title: Health Disparities and Health Equity

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Difference and disparity are not the same word. Two groups can differ on a health measure for many reasons, including age structure or ordinary random variation. It becomes a disparity when the difference tracks a pattern of disadvantage: who has stable housing, who lives within reach of a clinic, who has been treated unfairly by institutions. The test is not how large the gap is but whether it follows those fault lines. That distinction is practical, because it points the response toward the obstacles rather than toward the people experiencing them.

### Question 2

Equity concerns the chance a person has, not the identical package they receive. Healthy People 2030 sets the bar at everyone attaining their highest level of health, and WHO narrows the target to differences that are avoidable. So the question to ask of a program is not whether everyone got the same thing, but whether anything preventable stood between a person and their best possible health and whether it was removed. Identical services can leave a barrier fully standing: a clinic that charges nothing is equally free to everyone and still equally unreachable to someone two bus transfers away.

### Question 3

Equality is judged at the starting line and equity at the finish. Giving every clinic the same budget is simple to defend and simple to audit, but it preserves whatever gaps already exist. Equity deliberately allocates unevenly, sending more where the barrier is larger, and is evaluated by whether the gap actually narrows. The trap worth noticing is the middle case: allocating unevenly is not automatically equitable. Pouring extra events into the neighborhood that already screens the most is unequal and still pushes in the wrong direction.

### Question 4

Inequality is a measurement word and inequity is a judgment word. You can count an inequality without taking any position on it: older adults have more cataracts than twenty-year-olds, and that is simply true. Calling something an inequity adds two further claims, that it is unfair and that it could have gone otherwise. Every inequity is also an inequality, but the reverse does not hold. Collapsing the two makes it impossible to argue about which gaps genuinely demand action, because every observed difference would automatically qualify.

### Question 5

One term is about the service and the other about the result. Whether a patient received a timely referral, a qualified interpreter, or the guideline-recommended medication describes the care delivered, which makes it a health care disparity. Whether that patient's blood pressure ends up controlled, or whether they die earlier, describes health status, which makes it a health disparity. The distinction is operational: if the gap sits in care delivered, the levers are inside the organization, such as staffing, referral pathways, and language services. If outcomes diverge despite comparable care, the levers mostly sit outside it.

### Question 6

Coverage is the price of admission, not the experience that follows. Two patients holding the same card can meet very different systems: one clinic has a specialist on site and a staff interpreter, while the other refers out to a practice with a three-month wait. Layer on differences in how the same reported symptoms get interpreted by clinicians, and outcomes diverge without a single line of coverage changing. This is why expanding insurance narrows some gaps but rarely closes them. It removes one barrier out of several, and the remaining ones live in how care is actually delivered.

### Question 7

An intervention that lifts everyone by the same amount leaves the ranking exactly where it started: the average improves and the gap does not. Worse, anything requiring resources people already hold unevenly, such as a smartphone, broadband, or time away from work, gets taken up fastest at the top and can widen the gap while looking like progress on the headline number. The design that reliably narrows a gap is universal in reach but graded in intensity: offer it to everyone, then concentrate staffing, outreach, and follow-up where outcomes are worst.

### Question 8

An average is one number standing in for an entire distribution, and it can rise while the bottom of that distribution falls, because the top pulled hard enough to carry it. Nothing about the countywide figure is false; it is simply answering a different question than the equity question. Stratifying means recomputing the same indicator separately within groups defined by income, race and ethnicity, disability, or geography, so you can see whether the improvement actually reached the people furthest behind or merely reached the largest number of people.

### Question 9

Sort these examples by asking who acted. If the difference lies in something the delivery system did, such as who was referred, who received an interpreter, or who was offered the recommended medication, it is a health care disparity. If it lies in how healthy people are, such as weight, hearing, or activity level, it is a health disparity. The referral example is the cleanest because it holds clinical need constant: the patients presented with comparable symptoms, so the divergence sits in the decision made about them rather than in the disease itself.

### Question 10

Two different kinds of authority are being compared here. Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act is law, and its regulations say a health program that accepts federal money must take reasonable steps so a patient with limited English can actually use its services, which in practice usually means a qualified interpreter or translated materials at no cost to the patient. The CLAS Standards are a blueprint from the HHS Office of Minority Health describing what culturally and linguistically appropriate care looks like in practice. Knowing which is which tells you what an organization must do as opposed to what it should do.

### Question 11

Run both calculations on the same four numbers. Subtracting, the gap goes from 20 minus 10, which is 10 per 1,000, down to 10 minus 5, which is 5 per 1,000, so it halved. Dividing, 20 over 10 equals 2, and 10 over 5 still equals 2, so nothing moved. Neither result is wrong; they answer different questions. The absolute difference tells you how many extra events per 1,000 people the disadvantaged group carries, which sizes the harm on the table. The ratio tells you how many times the risk is, which indicates whether the underlying inequity has budged. Reporting only one is how the same decade gets described as either a success or a stalemate.

### Question 12

A single score does two damaging things at once here. It hides variation inside each site, because a site can post an acceptable average while one subgroup slips further behind. And when money follows that score without adjusting for who the site actually serves, resources drain away from the settings treating the hardest-to-reach patients, which are the clinics that would need more staff and outreach, not less, to close a gap. Correcting it takes two moves together: report results broken out by patient group, and account for social risk when the score determines payment.
